title: ER to Relational Mapping
description: Translate conceptual identities, attribute collections and relationships into explicit relational contracts, distinguishing conventional mapping patterns from complete constraint enforcement.
notes:
## Preserve meaning while changing representation

ER-to-relational mapping translates a conceptual model into relations, attributes, keys, and supported integrity mechanisms. The goal is to preserve the intended occurrences and relationships, not merely turn every diagram shape into an independent table. A good mapping explains which tuples represent entities, which represent participation facts, and how each complete identity survives the translation.

Start with the actual requirements. Student can mean a person role or a separately identified institutional record. Enrollment can mean a current pair, one offering, or a historical attempt. Room can be identified within a building. Those meanings determine keys and references. A mapping recipe applied without the occurrence grain can produce valid SQL that stores the wrong facts or rejects legitimate ones.

## Strong entities commonly become keyed relations

A straightforward strong-entity mapping creates a relation for the entity type, with suitable columns for its properties and a primary or other appropriate identifying constraint. Student(student_id, student_name) can represent independently identified students. Descriptive names remain nonunique if different students may share them. The key comes from the model's guarantee rather than from whichever column happens to be first.

Attribute domains require appropriate SQL types and supported constraints. Required values need an absence policy, and a broad integer or string type may not express the complete business rule. The mapping should identify those remaining obligations explicitly. A table definition with a primary key is not proof that every stored descriptive value is true or that every actor may access the entity.

## Composite properties map through meaningful roles

A single-valued Address can expose street_line, city, region, and postal_code as component columns under a chosen mapping. Nested conceptual components can be flattened into clearly named leaf roles. The grouping may no longer appear as one SQL column, but its meaning and component validity policy must remain consistent in the content and callers.

Multiple component columns do not imply multiple addresses. If a student may have several complete addresses, multiplicity needs an occurrence relation or another deliberate representation. Do not confuse a composite attribute with a composite key: a structured address need not identify the student, while an identifying pair need not represent one composite descriptive property.

## Collections commonly become owner-value relations

A multivalued phone property can map to StudentPhone(student_id, phone_number), with one current membership per tuple. A combined key can prevent repeated identical memberships while permitting several phones per student and a shared phone across students if the domain allows it. Parent existence needs an appropriate supported reference rule separately.

An empty collection can be represented by no child rows rather than one artificial NULL token. Modern SQL products can support structured collection values, but that is another design choice with its own constraint and query trade-offs. The conventional relation here makes independent membership explicit and avoids informal delimiter parsing. Its suitability follows the actual requirements rather than a blanket claim that collections can never occur inside supported SQL types.

## Weak identities include the owner context

In the Building-Room example, Room uses building_id and room_number together because the local number is unique only within an owner. The conventional mapping includes both in the Room primary key and uses building_id as a required reference to Building. Capacity remains descriptive. Two buildings can legitimately contain a room numbered 101.

A physical surrogate room_id can coexist with the required unique owner-number combination if the implementation needs that reference convenience. It does not make duplicate business room identities acceptable. The mapping must preserve the documented identifying dependency and lifecycle. Weakness does not automatically mandate cascade deletion; a supported restriction can preserve valid states while dependent rooms remain.

## One-to-many places the reference carefully

For Department offers Course, a common mapping puts department_id on the many-side Course relation. Each course can then store one current department assignment. A required valid assignment needs both required-value policy and supported parent-reference enforcement. The department identifier is normally allowed to repeat across different courses when one department can offer many courses.

Adding UNIQUE on Course.department_id would impose a different maximum. Likewise, requiring a valid department for each course does not require every department to offer a course. The parent-side minimum is a separate rule. Read the diagram's upper and lower participation bounds independently before choosing scalar references, uniqueness declarations, or additional trusted enforcement.

## One-to-one also needs the second maximum

A department-keyed HeadAssignment relation can ensure at most one head per department. If each faculty member may head at most one department, faculty_id needs an independent uniqueness guarantee in that population. Parent references and total head assignment for every department remain separate obligations. The two maximums do not automatically establish either side's minimum.

A nullable foreign reference can be useful for an optional one-to-one role under actual engine rules. It is not interchangeable with a required candidate identity without an appropriate absence policy. Explain the selected representation and exact permitted states rather than assuming all uniqueness declarations treat NULL identically across every database product or provider.

## Many-to-many requires explicit participation facts

A conventional Student-Course mapping uses an Enrollment relation containing participant references and relationship-specific properties. A combined key can identify one current enrollment per pair under that policy. If repeated attempts or offerings must coexist, the identity must distinguish them. The relationship's score belongs to that participation, not to a universal single Student score.

```sql
SELECT s.student_id, s.student_name, e.course_id
FROM students s
JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.student_id
ORDER BY s.student_id, e.course_id;
```

This returns relationship-grain rows, so a student's name can appear several times correctly. The mapping does not justify adding arbitrary DISTINCT to suppress real participation. A separate association relation preserves independently manageable links on both sides without relying on an informal list string or a fixed number of unrelated slots.

## Higher-level abstractions need complete references

An aggregated enrollment monitored by Faculty can map to a Monitoring relation referencing the existing enrollment identity. If the policy allows only one monitor, a scalar reference on Enrollment may fit instead. The conceptual aggregation does not select the multiplicity automatically. The mapping must preserve that monitoring names a specific existing association occurrence.

Subtype hierarchies also have several mapping strategies. Separate common and role tables can preserve shared Person identity and overlapping memberships. A single-table discriminator can fit some disjoint classifications. Neither automatically proves every completeness or exclusivity rule. Record the particular hierarchy constraints and where they are enforced, especially when rules span relations.

## Derived values need an authority contract

A derived age or total can be calculated in a query or view from authoritative inputs. It can also be cached or recorded as a deliberate snapshot with a defined consistency policy. Omitting an independently edited duplicate often avoids drift, but the word derived does not universally forbid stored results. The chosen implementation must explain reference time, source grain, and refresh semantics.

A stored cached total needs coverage of relevant source changes, not just one successful update example. A historical award may need its original recorded amount instead of a changed current catalogue value. Mapping is therefore partly about identifying authority: which facts are sources, which are calculations, and what exactly the stored or displayed result means.

## Validate the mapping with allowed and rejected states

Use repeated names, an empty parent category, several child links, duplicated proposed identities, missing optional values, and absent references. Test that legitimate individual-component reuse remains possible under combined keys and that invalid complete collisions fail. A fixture with one fully connected row cannot expose many incorrect maximums or missing owner components.

The exercises verify a student-course participation query and a local composite uniqueness declaration on synthetic SQL fixtures. Native reference behaviour, aggregate minimums, hierarchy transitions, exact MySQL/provider execution, and production authorization require their own evidence. A dependable mapping keeps conceptual identity, multiplicity, property ownership, and enforcement responsibilities consistent, making the resulting relations a faithful implementation contract rather than a mechanical inventory of diagram shapes.

questions.question_text: What is ER-to-Relational Mapping?
options: The process of drawing an ER diagram from an existing database
The systematic process of converting a completed ER/EER diagram into relational tables following defined rules
A way to normalize an already-existing relational schema
A technique for writing SQL queries
questions.explanation: This mapping bridges conceptual ER/EER design and the physical relational schema.

questions.question_text: How does a strong entity set typically map to a relational table?
options: Its attributes become columns and its key becomes the table's primary key
It is discarded and merged into relationships
It always requires a junction table
It becomes a foreign key in another table
questions.explanation: A strong entity set maps directly and simply to a table using its own attributes and key.

questions.question_text: In the conventional owner-plus-partial-key weak-entity mapping taught here, how is its complete identity represented?
options: They are mapped identically
The weak entity's table must include the owner's primary key as a foreign key, and its own primary key is a composite of the owner's key plus its partial key
Weak entity tables never have any foreign keys
Weak entity tables cannot have a primary key at all
questions.explanation: The mapped pair includes the owner key and discriminator with supported owner reference enforcement; alternative physical surrogates must preserve the business identity explicitly.

questions.question_text: How is a 1:N relationship (e.g., Department Offers Course) typically mapped, without needing a separate table?
options: By adding a foreign key column (e.g., Dept_Code) into the table on the 'many' side (Course)
By creating a junction table regardless
By merging Department and Course into one table always
By making Course a multi-valued attribute of Department
questions.explanation: For 1:N, a single foreign key on the many side is sufficient and standard.

questions.question_text: Why does the conventional normalized mapping use a separate association relation for an M:N enrollment?
options: Because M:N relationships never have attributes
It represents each independently manageable participation with complete participant references, identity and relationship properties
Because M:N relationships are always weak entities
Because SQL forbids M:N relationships entirely
questions.explanation: Structured SQL types exist, but an informal list is not equivalent to the explicit conventional relationship mapping and constraints.

questions.question_text: What generally happens to a derived attribute (like Age) during ER-to-relational mapping?
options: It always gets its own dedicated column
It is typically NOT given a stored column; it is recomputed via queries or views from its source attributes
It becomes a foreign key
It becomes the primary key of a new table
questions.explanation: Computing on demand can avoid independent drift. Deliberate caches or snapshots are also possible when authority and refresh or reference-state policies are defined.

questions.question_text: Which of these is NOT one of the standard strategies for mapping a generalization/specialization hierarchy to tables?
options: Superclass table plus one table per subclass, linked by a shared key
One single combined table with nullable subclass-specific columns
One table per subclass only, duplicating superclass attributes into each
Always deleting the superclass and keeping only a multi-valued attribute
questions.explanation: This is not a real mapping strategy; the three legitimate strategies are the other three options listed.

questions.question_text: When an enrollment can have several faculty monitors, which mapping preserves monitoring of its specific association occurrence?
options: A separate Monitoring relation referencing the complete existing enrollment identity and the faculty identity
By creating an entirely new unrelated table with no foreign keys
Aggregation cannot be mapped to relational tables at all
By duplicating the Faculty table's data into Student and Course
questions.explanation: A scalar Faculty_ID on Enrollment only fits an at-most-one-monitor policy; aggregation itself does not determine that multiplicity.

questions.question_text: What should a mapping preserve before choosing table shapes?
options: Only the number of drawn ovals
Occurrence meaning, complete identity and relationships
Only the shortest column names
Only the current sample row count
questions.explanation: Representation must preserve the intended facts.

questions.question_text: Why can UNIQUE on Course.department_id be wrong in a one-to-many mapping?
options: It makes course_id nullable automatically
It creates all department rows
It forbids several courses sharing one department
It changes the course title
questions.explanation: The many-side reference normally can repeat.

questions.question_text: Does a child foreign key require at least one child for every parent?
options: Yes; it inserts a child automatically
Only for integer keys
No; parent-side minimums are separate
Only if the table is empty
questions.explanation: Existence of referenced parents differs from participation coverage.

questions.question_text: What identifies Room under the stated weak mapping?
options: room_number globally
capacity alone
The row display offset
building_id and room_number together
questions.explanation: The owner completes the discriminator.

questions.question_text: Does a composite Address imply several address occurrences?
options: No; components and multiplicity differ
Yes; one component always means one address
Only if street is required
Only if city names repeat
questions.explanation: The property can be composite and single-valued.

questions.question_text: What can represent an empty current phone collection?
options: One compulsory zero phone
No owner-value membership rows
A different student identity
A missing Student definition
questions.explanation: Absent membership differs from a stored missing token.

questions.question_text: Where should a course-specific enrollment score be stored conceptually?
options: As a universal Student score
On the department name
On the participation occurrence
As the course primary identifier
questions.explanation: Attribute ownership follows the correct grain.

questions.question_text: What changes if several historical attempts of one course must coexist?
options: All scores must become keys
The student identity must change each time
A pair key is automatically sufficient
Enrollment identity must distinguish the intended occurrences
questions.explanation: Fact grain determines complete identity.

questions.question_text: Does a separate subtype table automatically enforce total specialization?
options: No; it need not create a role for every Person
Yes; every parent receives a subtype automatically
Only if names differ
Only if the role table is empty
questions.explanation: Hierarchy coverage needs an explicit enforcement account.

questions.question_text: Can a derived result be stored deliberately?
options: No; any storage makes derivation impossible
Yes, with an explicit authoritative calculation and consistency or snapshot policy
Only if every source is NULL
Only if it is a key
questions.explanation: Conceptual source dependence and physical storage differ.

questions.question_text: Why test repeated individual components under a composite key?
options: To force every row to duplicate
To remove references
To ensure legitimate combinations are not rejected by mistaken single-column uniqueness
To change relation degree
questions.explanation: The complete combination, not each component, is identifying.

questions.question_text: What does a local uniqueness fixture not establish?
options: The exercised duplicate error
The selected fixture output
The recorded composite identity
Every native reference, hierarchy and production access rule
questions.explanation: Evidence must match the actual tested boundary.

coding_problems.title: Read the mapped student-course association
coding_problems.task: Return student_id, student_name and course_id for every matching enrollment. Preserve students’ distinct course participation and repeated names.
coding_problems.schema_sql:
CREATE TABLE students (student_id INT PRIMARY KEY, student_name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id INT NOT NULL, course_id INT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY(student_id,course_id));
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO students VALUES (1,'Asha'),(2,'Asha'),(3,'Mira'); INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (1,10),(1,20),(2,10);
coding_problems.expected:
student_id	student_name	course_id
1	Asha	10
1	Asha	20
2	Asha	10
constraints: All supplied enrollment parent references are valid; temporary mirrors do not verify native reference enforcement.
edge_cases: A student can have several participation facts.
An unenrolled student is absent from this participation listing.
hints: Join using the modeled student identity.
Retain course_id rather than collapsing the result to names.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT s.student_id, s.student_name, e.course_id FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.student_id ORDER BY s.student_id, e.course_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The mapping preserves independent entity identity and a separate relation for the stated participation grain.

validation_cases.seed_sql: INSERT INTO students VALUES (7,'Mira'); INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (7,10),(7,20);

coding_problems.title: Enforce the mapped current participation identity
coding_problems.task: The policy permits one current enrollment per student-course pair. Add UNIQUE(student_id, course_id) named enrollment_pair to registrations, preserving its internal registration_id primary key. Return all three identifiers.
coding_problems.starter_sql: -- Add the combined participation uniqueness rule and return registrations.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE registrations (registration_id INT PRIMARY KEY, student_id INT NOT NULL, course_id INT NOT NULL);
constraints: Initial pairs satisfy the proposed rule.
The exercise does not model repeated attempts; native parent existence and production registration authority are separate.
edge_cases: One student can take different courses.
A new internal id must not permit the same business pair.
hints: Do not constrain either participant independently as unique.
coding_problems.solution_sql:
ALTER TABLE registrations ADD CONSTRAINT enrollment_pair UNIQUE (student_id, course_id);
SELECT registration_id, student_id, course_id FROM registrations ORDER BY registration_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The independent business-pair rule preserves the conceptual current enrollment identity alongside the physical primary identifier.

negative_validation_cases.sql: UPDATE registrations SET course_id=10 WHERE registration_id=2;

original_questions.question_text: How does a strong entity set typically map to a relational table?

original_questions.question_text: How does a weak entity set's table differ from a strong entity set's table?
options: They are mapped identically
The weak entity's table must include the owner's primary key as a foreign key, and its own primary key is a composite of the owner's key plus its partial key
Weak entity tables never have any foreign keys
Weak entity tables cannot have a primary key at all
original_questions.explanation: This directly reflects the weak entity's dependence on its owner for full identification.

original_questions.question_text: How is a 1:N relationship (e.g., Department Offers Course) typically mapped, without needing a separate table?
options: By adding a foreign key column (e.g., Dept_Code) into the table on the 'many' side (Course)
By creating a junction table regardless
By merging Department and Course into one table always
By making Course a multi-valued attribute of Department
original_questions.explanation: For 1:N, a single foreign key on the many side is sufficient and standard.

original_questions.question_text: Why does an M:N relationship require its own separate junction table, unlike 1:N?
options: Because M:N relationships never have attributes
Because neither side's table can hold a variable-length list of foreign keys to represent multiple simultaneous links on both sides
Because M:N relationships are always weak entities
Because SQL forbids M:N relationships entirely
original_questions.explanation: A junction table with composite foreign keys is needed since both sides can have many corresponding rows.

original_questions.question_text: What generally happens to a derived attribute (like Age) during ER-to-relational mapping?
options: It always gets its own dedicated column
It is typically NOT given a stored column; it is recomputed via queries or views from its source attributes
It becomes a foreign key
It becomes the primary key of a new table
original_questions.explanation: Since derived attributes are computable from other stored data, they are usually left out of the physical schema to avoid redundancy.

original_questions.question_text: Which of these is NOT one of the standard strategies for mapping a generalization/specialization hierarchy to tables?
options: Superclass table plus one table per subclass, linked by a shared key
One single combined table with nullable subclass-specific columns
One table per subclass only, duplicating superclass attributes into each
Always deleting the superclass and keeping only a multi-valued attribute
original_questions.explanation: This is not a real mapping strategy; the three legitimate strategies are the other three options listed.

original_questions.question_text: How is an aggregation (e.g., Faculty Monitored_By the Student-Enrolls_In-Course pairing) typically mapped to tables?
options: By adding a foreign key (e.g., Faculty_ID) directly into the junction table that already represents the aggregated relationship (e.g., Enrollment)
By creating an entirely new unrelated table with no foreign keys
Aggregation cannot be mapped to relational tables at all
By duplicating the Faculty table's data into Student and Course
original_questions.explanation: Since the junction table (Enrollment) already represents the aggregated relationship as rows, adding a foreign key to it is the natural mapping.

review.notes_review: Definitions and examples checked against questions; no plagiarism certification.

batch_review.scope: New package only: notes, keyed examples, original question identities and canonical indices, every correct answer, exercises and recorded fixture outputs, diagram trace, content-only paired integration.
batch_review.findings_resolved: Outer Join retained absence question clarified: missing parent is a violation only when the modeled relationship requires it. Division retains its original Hard exercise; validator permits retained Hard alongside Easy while rejecting a new Hard substitute.
batch_review.remaining: Exact MySQL/provider execution, browser QA, independent review and applied-migration behavior unverified; output fixtures do not prove required source technique.

diagrams.caption: Different conceptual rules require different relational mechanisms
diagrams.description: The mapping separates identity, reference existence, multiplicity and derived authority rather than assuming one table declaration enforces the entire diagram.
rows: Complete occurrence identity and parent existence
